guest.bio_context: Terry Riggs started in the building and construction industry in 1971 as a builder's labourer in Sale, East Gippsland, before transitioning to scaffolding ten years later. He worked on major projects including Barry Beach offshore construction from 1978 to 1983, where he gained expertise in complex metal scaffold construction. He obtained both scaffolding and rigging qualifications, worked at the Shell Refinery in 1990, and has been a contract scaffolder across numerous commercial and suburban construction sites throughout Victoria and Western Australia since the 1980s.

pending_qa.q: How did custom and practice function as safety and skill transmission in pre-regulation scaffolding work?
pending_qa.r: Custom and practice was the act in circumstances where there was no act, and it was actually more powerful than formal regulations. Experienced scaffolders took their job seriously, kept a close eye on newer workers, and imparted knowledge directly. The most important thing was having a good lead hand who would teach you to be part of a gang and ensure you knew what you were doing before moving you up in the air.

pending_qa.q: What were the physical toll and occupational health impacts on contract scaffolders carrying heavy loads?
pending_qa.r: Most scaffolders wore out their knees or backs from carrying heavy, concentrated loads, typically on one shoulder without alternating much. A right-handed scaffolder would carry the load on the right shoulder, putting a big load on the right knee, which eventually failed for most people. The cumulative vertical strain from knees to hips to shoulders meant something in the system would eventually fail because 95% of scaffolding work involves carrying tons of steel either to or away from the job.

pending_qa.q: What safety risks emerged from scaffold construction methods using boom lifts instead of conventional hanging methods?
pending_qa.r: When a scaffold was built using a boom lift rather than conventional construction as a hanging scaffold, fittings were not all done up properly. Terry experienced a frightening incident in Port Hedland around 1998 at a 70-metre tower where a tube dropped because while the ledger fitting was done up, the transom fitting was not, and it fell. Without a protrusion from the vessel breaking the fall, he and his off-sider would have come off the scaffold.

pending_qa.q: What structural failures occur when scaffold standards are not staggered properly?
pending_qa.r: When standards are not staggered and joins all align on one level, the scaffold can fail catastrophically. Terry saw a clattered demolition scaffold on Russell Street in the 1980s where the standards came out of the spigots on the building side because they didn't stagger them, and it hung into Russell Street. This represents a loss and discounting of skill and knowledge in how scaffolds are erected.

pending_qa.q: How essential was interpersonal cooperation and gang cohesion to effective scaffolding work?
pending_qa.r: Scaffolding is not an individual pursuit, and one experienced scaffolder told Terry that if you can't get on with people, you're no good, no matter if you're a super scaffolder—they'll just get rid of you and get two other people. You need to cooperate and be on the same page with the three or two men you're working with because if you're not, something's likely to go wrong, and the thing Terry worried about most was people invading his space because they could make a mistake and push him over the side.

pending_qa.q: What role did the monthly scaffold meetings at Trades Hall play in maintaining industry standards and knowledge sharing?
pending_qa.r: The scaffold meetings at Trades Hall, chaired by Normie Wallace, were held in the round with people sitting on wooden benches in a semicircle facing each other, creating a family-gathering atmosphere. These meetings were a good place to learn custom and practice through debate and discussion, and Normie Wallace was unbelievable at pulling people up when they were talking shit or mentioning someone doing something wrong, ensuring rank-and-file involvement held people accountable based on actual experience.
